title: Al-Haouz Earthquake Misinformation Crisis in Morocco: A Content Analysis of Tweets on X
screen_reason: Manual content/veracity analysis of a hashtag-defined corpus of tweets about the September 2023 Al-Haouz earthquake; reports the share of the analysed tweets coded as misinformation (512 of 5,594; 9%), i.e. a CONTENT prevalence estimate with an explicit denominator.

estimates.measure_type: % of Al-Haouz earthquake tweets coded as misinformation
estimates.value_raw: misinformation (n=512) of 5,594 analysed tweets = 9.2%; paper reports 'misinformation (9%)' vs 'not-misinformation (91%)'
estimates.denominator: 5,594 earthquake-related tweets retained for analysis (from 9,057 collected via earthquake hashtags in Arabic, French, English and Spanish)
estimates.definition: Tweet labelled 'misinformation' in a manual veracity analysis: content reviewed, claims traced on fact-checking platforms and by reverse image search, cross-checked against verified data and official reports, then labelled misinformation or not-misinformation
estimates.misinfo_def: 'information that is false or misleading according to the best available evidence at the time and that is communicated regardless of an intention to deceive' (Dallo et al., 2022, p.2), used to cover both misinformation and disinformation
estimates.source_quote: After the filtering process of the dataset (n=9057), only 5594 tweets were considered for analysis, given the majority of non-representative tweets were removed, e.g. irrelevant, deleted, or duplicated tweets. The tweets were then categorized into misinformation (n=512) and not-misinformation (n=5082).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Frequency of Misinformation and Not-misinformation Tweets', pp. 25-26; Figure 2
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two media and communication PhD researchers coded a random subset of 200 tweets; Cohen's kappa = 0.49 for the misinformation vs not-misinformation distinction (theme kappas 0.41-0.94). Veracity was established by tracing claims on AFP Fact Check, Misbar, Fatabayano, Reuters Fact Check and Snopes, by Google reverse image search, and via X's Community Notes.
estimates.moderator_quote: The data was extracted using the hashtags #earthquakemorocco, ... #MarrakeshEarthquake, #moroccoearthquake, ... # Morocco, and #earthquake within the timeframe from 8 September to 31 December, 2023. The extraction process resulted in 9,057 tweets in Arabic, French, English, and Spanish for analysis
estimates.notes: Second verbatim span for the same value (quoted here because source_quote must be one contiguous span): 'As illustrated in Figure 2, the highest percentage of not-misinformation (91%) in relation to misinformation (9%) is substantial, indicating the accuracy of tweets about the Al-Haouz earthquake discourse on X.' Topic is a natural disaster / crisis-communication corpus, coded 'other' (no earthquake/disaster category). Country coded Morocco because the corpus is defined by the Moroccan earthquake, but tweets were multilingual and posters' locations are not reported, so this is the topic's country rather than a sampled national population. Value computed as the exact part/whole share of the two verbatim counts (512/5,594); the paper's own rounded figure is 9%.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: the misinformation-theme breakdown in Table 1 (sensationalist reporting 308/514 = 60%, misleading visual representation 157 = 31%, conspiracy theory 28 = 5%, pseudoscientific explanation 14 = 3%, false prediction 7 = 1%). These are shares computed INSIDE the misinformation-only subsample and describe the composition of misinformation types, not the prevalence of misinformation in any population of items, so they carry no prevalence meaning; if the review wants them they would be within_misinfo_content=true appendix rows. Also not extracted: fact-checking tweets (n=25) among the not-misinformation category (a count with no clean share reported); the monthly counts read off Figures 3-4 (approximations, described in prose as 'approximately 4,500', 'fewer than 100' - not verbatim values); and modality counts of misinformation tweets (text 247, video 159, picture 106), again a within-misinformation composition. The Vosoughi et al. '70% of online users could not differentiate' figure is cited from elsewhere and is excluded by R8.

rob.design: Exploratory content analysis of 9,057 tweets pulled by a third party through the X API plus manual scraping using ten earthquake hashtags (Arabic, French, English, Spanish), 8 Sep - 31 Dec 2023; 5,594 retained after removing irrelevant, deleted and duplicate tweets. Two media/communication PhD researchers coded a random 200-tweet subset for reliability: Cohen's kappa = 0.49 (misinformation vs not), 0.51 sensationalist reporting, 0.68 conspiracy, 0.94 false prediction, 0.47 misleading visual, 0.41 pseudoscientific. Veracity was assessed manually against fact-checking sites, reverse image search and official reports. No sampling weights, no bot filtering (acknowledged), no account-level or engagement-weighted analysis; author states the study is not generalizable.
